items.stem: Why can equilibrium only be reached in a closed system?
options: Otherwise products or reactants escape and the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
items.answer: Otherwise products or reactants escape and the reverse reaction cannot keep pace
items.markingKey: A. e.g. gases escaping.

items.stem: Distinguish between dynamic equilibrium and static equilibrium.
items.answer: In static equilibrium nothing is moving (a balanced seesaw); in dynamic equilibrium forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
items.markingKey: In static equilibrium nothing is moving (a balanced seesaw); in dynamic equilibrium forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "At equilibrium the reaction has stopped." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Both reactions continue at equal rates – the equilibrium is dynamic.
items.markingKey: Both reactions continue at equal rates – the equilibrium is dynamic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Haemoglobin and oxygen, explain how it illustrates reversible reactions in the body.
items.answer: Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly: in the lungs (high O₂) oxyhaemoglobin forms; in respiring tissues (low O₂) oxygen is released. A reversible equilibrium allows the same molecule to load and unload oxygen.
items.markingKey: Context (Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly: in the lungs (high O₂) oxyhaemoglobin forms; in respiring tissues (low O₂) oxygen is released.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A reversible equilibrium allows the same molecule to load and unload oxygen. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reversible reactions in the body.

items.stem: Lars wants to find out how the temperature affects the colour of an equilibrium mixture of cobalt chloride complexes. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does temperature of the water bath affect absorbance of the solution at 650 nm?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (temperature of the water bath (0, 20, 40, 60, 80 °C)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (absorbance of the solution at 650 nm (blue complex) measured with a colorimeter) in a question form.

items.stem: Describe what happens to the rates and concentrations from the start of a reversible reaction until dynamic equilibrium is reached, and explain why this only happens in a closed system.
items.answer: At start only reactants: forward rate high, backward zero. As reactants are used, forward rate falls; products build up, backward rate rises. Eventually rates are equal – concentrations constant – dynamic equilibrium; both reactions continue. A closed system is needed so that no reactants or products escape; otherwise the backward reaction cannot balance the forward.
items.markingKey: At start only reactants: forward rate high, backward zero. As reactants are used, forward rate falls; products build up, backward rate rises. Eventually rates are equal – concentrations constant – dynamic equilibrium; both reactions continue. A closed system is needed so that no reactants or products escape; otherwise the backward reaction cannot balance the forward.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A system in which no substances can enter or leave"?
items.answer: closed system
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of closed system.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "closed system"?
options: A system in which no substances can enter or leave
If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change
The equilibrium position moves towards the products
Returning unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen to the reactor to increase overall conversion
items.answer: A system in which no substances can enter or leave
items.markingKey: A. "closed system" is a system in which no substances can enter or leave.

items.stem: Explain why a reversible reaction in an open beaker may go to completion.
items.answer: If a gaseous product escapes, the backward reaction cannot occur, so the forward reaction continues until the reactant is used up.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If a gaseous product escapes, the backward reaction cannot occur, so the forward reaction continues until the reactant is used up. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why heating blue copper sulfate is endothermic but adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate is exothermic.
items.answer: In a reversible reaction the energy change in one direction is equal and opposite to the other.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In a reversible reaction the energy change in one direction is equal and opposite to the other. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Kwame monitored the concentration of product in a reversible reaction in a sealed flask over time (three runs).

Time / min | Product concentration / mol/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3

4 | 0.411 | 0.408 | 0.390
8 | 0.564 | 0.530 | 0.542

State the time at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 8 min; range = 0.034 mol/dm³; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 8 min; 1 range = max − min = 0.564 − 0.530 = 0.034 mol/dm³; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Freya plans to investigate how the temperature affects the colour of an equilibrium mixture of cobalt chloride complexes. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: concentration of cobalt chloride and HCl; volume in each cuvette; time at each temperature (5 min); calibration with a blank

items.stem: The forward reaction is exothermic. What happens to the yield if temperature is increased?
items.answer: It decreases
items.markingKey: It decreases. Equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction.

items.stem: "A catalyst increases the amount of product at equilibrium." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally so the yield is unchanged; equilibrium is reached sooner.
items.markingKey: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally so the yield is unchanged; equilibrium is reached sooner. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the rate of reaching equilibrium and the position of equilibrium.
items.answer: The position (yield) depends on concentration, pressure and temperature; the rate depends on temperature, pressure, concentration and catalysts.
items.markingKey: The position (yield) depends on concentration, pressure and temperature; the rate depends on temperature, pressure, concentration and catalysts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Yusuf analysed data for the percentage of ammonia at equilibrium at 400 °C at different pressures (three data sources).

Pressure / atm | Ammonia at equilibrium / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
50 | 15 | 15 | 14
100 | 24 | 25 | 23
200 | 36 | 34 | 35
300 | 43 | 42 | 41
400 | 46 | 45 | 46

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The percentage of ammonia at equilibrium increases with pressure, but the increase gets smaller at higher pressures. The forward reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ reduces the number of gas moles from 4 to 2, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier).
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The percentage of ammonia at equilibrium increases with pressure, but the increase gets smaller at higher pressures.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: The forward reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ reduces the number of gas moles from 4 to 2, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier).

items.stem: Alessia is investigating how the concentration of added iron(III) ions affects the colour of the iron(III) thiocyanate equilibrium. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ iron(III) chloride added (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 drops to 10 cm³ mixture)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ iron(III) chloride added (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 drops to 10 cm³ mixture) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into how the concentration of added iron(III) ions affects the colour of the iron(III) thiocyanate equilibrium.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how time before reading (2 min) will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ iron(III) chloride added affect absorbance of the red complex at 470 nm? (b) volume of 0.1 mol/dm³ iron(III) chloride added (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 drops to 10 cm³ mixture) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) absorbance of the red complex at 470 nm; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) time before reading (2 min) – equilibrium must be re-established. (e) iron(III) chloride is corrosive and potassium thiocyanate harmful – gloves and eye protection.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why time before reading (2 min) is controlled (equilibrium must be re-established). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. iron(III) chloride is corrosive and potassium thiocyanate harmful – gloves and eye protection.

items.stem: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ/mol, predict and explain the effect on the yield of SO₃ of (a) increasing temperature, (b) increasing pressure, (c) adding a catalyst, (d) adding more O₂.
items.answer: (a) yield decreases – equilibrium shifts in endothermic (backward) direction to absorb heat; (b) yield increases – 3 moles of gas → 2, shift to fewer moles; (c) no change in yield, faster attainment; (d) yield increases – shifts right to use up added O₂.
items.markingKey: (a) yield decreases – equilibrium shifts in endothermic (backward) direction to absorb heat; (b) yield increases – 3 moles of gas → 2, shift to fewer moles; (c) no change in yield, faster attainment; (d) yield increases – shifts right to use up added O₂.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the concentration of added iron(III) ions affects the colour of the iron(III) thiocyanate equilibrium. items.answer: Key hazard(s): iron(III) chloride is corrosive and potassium thiocyanate harmful – gloves and eye protection. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.

items.answer: It is a powerful qualitative tool, but quantitative yields require equilibrium constant calculations.

items.stem: The equilibrium CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g) has ΔH = −91 kJ/mol. Recommend the conditions of temperature and pressure for making methanol industrially, explaining the effect of each on yield and rate, and the role of a catalyst.
items.answer: Pressure: 3 moles of gas → 1, so high pressure increases yield and rate; but costly and hazardous – choose moderately high (50–100 atm). Temperature: exothermic forward reaction, so low temperature gives high yield but slow rate – compromise about 250 °C. Catalyst (copper/zinc oxide) increases rate so a lower temperature can be used; no effect on yield. Remove methanol by condensing and recycle unreacted gases.
items.markingKey: Pressure: 3 moles of gas → 1, so high pressure increases yield and rate; but costly and hazardous – choose moderately high (50–100 atm). Temperature: exothermic forward reaction, so low temperature gives high yield but slow rate – compromise about 250 °C. Catalyst (copper/zinc oxide) increases rate so a lower temperature can be used; no effect on yield. Remove methanol by condensing and recycle unreacted gases.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "compromise conditions"?
options: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas
Conditions chosen to balance yield, rate, cost and safety, e.g. 450 °C and 200 atm for ammonia
A system in which no substances can enter or leave
The industrial process for sulfuric acid, including 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
items.answer: Conditions chosen to balance yield, rate, cost and safety, e.g. 450 °C and 200 atm for ammonia
items.markingKey: B. "compromise conditions" is conditions chosen to balance yield, rate, cost and safety, e.g. 450 °C and 200 atm for ammonia.

items.stem: Explain the environmental impacts of the Haber process.
items.answer: It uses about 1–2% of world energy and produces CO₂ from making hydrogen from methane; fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and N₂O emissions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It uses about 1–2% of world energy and produces CO₂ from making hydrogen from methane; fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and N₂O emissions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Industry always uses conditions that give the highest yield." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Industry chooses compromise conditions that give an acceptable yield quickly and economically and safely.
items.markingKey: Industry chooses compromise conditions that give an acceptable yield quickly and economically and safely. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch (1909–1913) shows science, benefits and ethics.
items.answer: Haber developed the ammonia synthesis in the laboratory; Bosch scaled it up industrially at BASF. Haber also led Germany’s chemical weapons programme in World War I. The process feeds billions but was also used to make explosives – showing that science can be used for good and harm.
items.markingKey: Context (Haber developed the ammonia synthesis in the laboratory; Bosch scaled it up industrially at BASF. Haber also led Germany’s chemical weapons programme in World War I.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The process feeds billions but was also used to make explosives – showing that science can be used for good and harm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to science, benefits and ethics.

items.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Calculate the maximum mass of ammonia that could be made from 140 tonnes of nitrogen (Mr N₂ = 28, NH₃ = 17).
items.answer: 170 tonnes
items.markingKey: M1 moles ratio: 28 t N₂ → 2 × 17 = 34 t NH₃; M1 140 × 34 ÷ 28; A1 170 tonnes.

items.answer: record both the yield and the rate (time to equilibrium) at each temperature

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "iron catalyst".

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Haber process and the Contact process.
items.answer: The Haber process makes ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst, ~450 °C, ~200 atm); the Contact process makes sulfuric acid via SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, ~450 °C, ~1–2 atm).

items.stem: Explain why only about 15% of the gases are converted to ammonia in each pass, yet the overall conversion is about 97%.
items.answer: Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the reactor many times, so eventually almost all are converted.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the reactor many times, so eventually almost all are converted. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Higher temperature increases the rate but decreases the yield (exothermic forward reaction); higher pressure increases both but costs more.

items.stem: In an investigation into how temperature affects the equilibrium yield of a model gas-phase reaction, using published data and a simulation, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: pressure (200 atm).
items.answer: pressure also affects yield

items.stem: Each pass converts 25% of the remaining reactants to ammonia, and unreacted gases are recycled. What percentage of the original reactants has been converted after 5 passes?
items.markingKey: M1 fraction left = (1 − 0.25)^5 = 0.237; M1 converted = 1 − 0.237; A1 76.3%.

items.stem: Explain the choice of conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst, removal of ammonia) in the Haber process, using ideas about rate, equilibrium position and cost.
items.answer: Exothermic forward reaction: low T favours yield but slow → compromise 450 °C. Fewer moles of gas on right: high P favours yield and rate, but expensive and dangerous → ~200 atm. Iron catalyst: faster rate at lower temperature, no effect on yield. Ammonia condensed and removed; unreacted gases recycled → ~97% overall conversion. Conditions balance acceptable yield, fast rate, and cost/safety.
items.markingKey: Exothermic forward reaction: low T favours yield but slow → compromise 450 °C. Fewer moles of gas on right: high P favours yield and rate, but expensive and dangerous → ~200 atm. Conditions balance acceptable yield, fast rate, and cost/safety.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Haemoglobin and oxygen shows reversible reactions in the body.
items.answer: Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly: in the lungs (high O₂) oxyhaemoglobin forms; in respiring tissues (low O₂) oxygen is released. A reversible equilibrium allows the same molecule to load and unload oxygen.
items.markingKey: Context (Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly: in the lungs (high O₂) oxyhaemoglobin forms; in respiring tissues (low O₂) oxygen is released.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A reversible equilibrium allows the same molecule to load and unload oxygen. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reversible reactions in the body.

items.stem: Alessia is investigating how the concentration of added iron(III) ions affects the colour of the iron(III) thiocyanate equilibrium. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If more Fe³⁺ is added, then the mixture will become darker red, because the equilibrium Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ shifts to the right to use up the added Fe³⁺.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If more Fe³⁺ is added, then the mixture will become darker red, because the equilibrium Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ shifts to the right to use up the added Fe³⁺.

items.stem:
Chloé monitored the concentration of product in a reversible reaction in a sealed flask over time (three runs).

Time / min | Product concentration / mol/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 0.248 | 0.248 | 0.233
4 | 0.390 | 0.396 | 0.391
8 | 0.519 | 0.549 | 0.511
12 | 0.579 | 0.571 | 0.568
20 | 0.599 | 0.605 | 0.625

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The product concentration increases quickly at first, then more slowly, and becomes constant at about 0.6 mol/dm³. As products build up the backward reaction speeds up and the forward reaction slows; when their rates are equal, dynamic equilibrium is reached and concentrations stay constant.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The product concentration increases quickly at first, then more slowly, and becomes constant at about 0.6 mol/dm³.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: As products build up the backward reaction speeds up and the forward reaction slows; when their rates are equal, dynamic equilibrium is reached and concentrations stay constant.

items.stem: Leila is investigating how temperature affects the equilibrium yield of a model gas-phase reaction, using published data and a simulation. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the temperature increases, then the equilibrium yield will decrease but equilibrium will be reached faster, because the forward reaction is exothermic but all reactions speed up at higher temperatures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the temperature increases, then the equilibrium yield will decrease but equilibrium will be reached faster, because the forward reaction is exothermic but all reactions speed up at higher temperatures.

items.stem: "Increasing temperature always increases yield." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It increases yield only if the forward reaction is endothermic; for exothermic forward reactions the yield falls.
items.markingKey: It increases yield only if the forward reaction is endothermic; for exothermic forward reactions the yield falls. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The “two beakers of water” model is a good way to explain dynamic equilibrium."
items.answer: It is a helpful model for dynamic equilibrium, but its limitations should be discussed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shows rates becoming equal and levels constant while transfer continues. Arguments against: beakers do not show particles or energy changes; can wrongly suggest equal amounts. Supported judgement: It is a helpful model for dynamic equilibrium, but its limitations should be discussed.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how temperature affects the equilibrium yield of a model gas-phase reaction, using published data and a simulation. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): no physical hazards in a simulation; consider screen breaks; real ammonia is toxic – never attempt high-pressure reactions in school. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. no physical hazards in a simulation; consider screen breaks; real ammonia is toxic – never attempt high-pressure reactions in school); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Le Chatelier’s principle can be used to predict exactly how much product will form." Discuss.
items.answer: It is a powerful qualitative tool, but quantitative yields require equilibrium constant calculations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: correctly predicts the direction of shift; useful for choosing conditions. Arguments against: it is qualitative – it does not give amounts; equilibrium constants are needed for quantitative predictions. Supported judgement: It is a powerful qualitative tool, but quantitative yields require equilibrium constant calculations. items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the temperature affects the colour of an equilibrium mixture of cobalt chloride complexes. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Prepare a pink cobalt chloride solution in hydrochloric acid; pour equal volumes into tubes; place in water baths at each temperature for 5 min; transfer quickly to cuvettes; measure absorbance at 650 nm; repeat three times; plot absorbance against temperature.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (cobalt chloride is toxic and a possible carcinogen – gloves, eye protection, avoid skin contact; concentrated HCl in a fume cupboard). Model: Prepare a pink cobalt chloride solution in hydrochloric acid; pour equal volumes into tubes; place in water baths at each temperature for 5 min; transfer quickly to cuvettes; measure absorbance at 650 nm; repeat three times; plot absorbance against temperature.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "effect of concentration"?
options: The equilibrium position moves towards the products
A reaction in which products can react to re-form the reactants, shown by ⇌
Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products, using it up
The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium
items.answer: Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products, using it up
items.markingKey: C. "effect of concentration" is adding a reactant shifts equilibrium towards the products, using it up.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium"?
items.answer: position of equilibrium
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of position of equilibrium.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The industrial process for sulfuric acid, including 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst"?
items.answer: Contact process

items.stem: For CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g) (forward reaction endothermic), what happens to the position of equilibrium if the temperature is increased?

Shifts to the right; more product
items.answer: Shifts to the right; more product

items.stem: Explain the difference between dynamic equilibrium and static equilibrium.
items.answer: In static equilibrium nothing is moving (a balanced seesaw); in dynamic equilibrium forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
items.markingKey: In static equilibrium nothing is moving (a balanced seesaw); in dynamic equilibrium forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the Haber process and the Contact process.
items.answer: The Haber process makes ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst, ~450 °C, ~200 atm); the Contact process makes sulfuric acid via SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, ~450 °C, ~1–2 atm).
items.markingKey: The Haber process makes ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst, ~450 °C, ~200 atm); the Contact process makes sulfuric acid via SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, ~450 °C, ~1–2 atm). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch (1909–1913) as an example, explain science, benefits and ethics.
items.answer: Haber developed the ammonia synthesis in the laboratory; Bosch scaled it up industrially at BASF. Haber also led Germany’s chemical weapons programme in World War I. The process feeds billions but was also used to make explosives – showing that science can be used for good and harm.
